title: How To Get Your Students' Attention Fast
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin argues that a reliable attention signal is a basic but critical teaching tool, and specifies his preferences within it: he avoids silent signals (raised fingers, finger-over-lips) because they take too long to register, and avoids call-and-response signals like clapping patterns because of unnecessary complexity, preferring a simple, unambiguous auditory cue such as the phrase 'Can I have your attention please.' The bulk of the piece is an eleven-step training sequence for teaching the signal: explain its purpose, model both giving and responding to it, set a concrete response-time expectation (he claims one second is achievable), then run repeated practice rounds where students simulate discussion using playful filler phrases before the signal is given, gradually varying timing before using the signal for real. He closes with an important caveat that limits the piece from being a mere procedural checklist: the technique only works on top of genuinely good classroom management, and if underlying management is weak, teaching the signal in isolation won't fix a chronically unresponsive class.

Vary the timing of practice rounds so the response becomes automatic rather than tied to a predictable rhythm.

quotes: The ability to get your students’ attention anytime you need it is critical for good teaching.
I don’t recommend silent signals like holding fingers in the air and/or placing the index finger over the lips because it takes too long for students to respond.
Personally, I prefer “Can I have your attention please” because there is no confusion. It’s simple and communicates exactly what you want.
Set your expectation. For example, you want them silent and facing you within one second. (Yes, this is doable.)
However, in the absence of good classroom management, it’s unlikely to work very well. You’ll have to wait and repeat yourself again and again.
Take care of this first. Learn and apply the basics of SCM before teaching your signal. In this way, it will work as it should.
